newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE - Bangladesh counts cost of trade liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bangladesh counts cost of trade liberalisation.

text.p: Until the government waived a ban on newsprint imports two years ago, Bangladesh's lone newsprint mill in southern Khulna district enjoyed an absolute monoply.
Newspapers used to queue up to make sure their monthly quota was not cut. Low cost publishers had to pay above market prices whenever there was a fluctuation in production.
Now that newsprint can be imported, the giant state-owned newsprint factory with nearly 2,500 employees is facing its worst crisis in its 38 years of operation.
The newspaper industry, the mill's major customer, has almost stopped using their quotas even though the government continues subsidising its newsprint at 5,600 taka per tonne .
Other consumers are also losing interest, saying imported newsprint is better, even at higher prices, because it is whiter, less coarse and nearly waste-free.
With demand shrinking drastically, the Khulna Newsprint Mill has been forced to reduce daily production to 40 tonnes from 140 tonnes.
"The existence of the factory is at stake. Unsold stocks are piling up everyday," said one senior executive of the mill.

The mill is not the only one facing tough competition with Bangladesh rapidly dismantling its barriers and liberalising its trade. To hundreds of factories that were surviving in a heavily protected market, trade liberalisation came as a death-knell.
TARIFF LIBERALISATION BEGAN YEARS AGO
Bangladesh began the process of tariff liberalisation in the mid-1980s but accelerated the pace from the early 1990s.

The highest customs duty was slashed to 45 percent in the current 1996/97 fiscal year (July-June) from 350 percent in 1991/92. Items on the import ban list were reduced to 24 from 451 during the period.
Industries relying on the domestic market suffered a serious blow as price-competitive foreign products of all kinds poured into Bangladesh, which has an annual per capita income of $240.
Official estimates say imports of consumer goods will reach 20 billion taka in 1996/97 from 6.64 billion in 1991/92.
Even many multinationals, producing only for the Bangladesh market, have cut back production and begun marketing products by importing from their low cost production bases.
As a result, dozens of small and medium textile units, steel re-rolling mills, low-priced cosmetics factories and detergent units have been forced to close.

"Things happened so abruptly that many industries died almost overnight," said Mushfiqur Rahman, a top executive of a cosmetics factory near Dhaka. "We are fighting for survival against a variety of imported Indian cosmetics."
A spokesman of the Bangladesh Sick Industries Rehabilitation Council claimed at least 5,000 factories had lost substantial shares of the domestic market and were now "sick".
Bangladesh's banking sector has accumulated outstanding loans of 130 billion taka ($3 billion), and sources say many companies defaulted because they could no longer sell their products.

"Many are wilful defaulters, but liberalisation forced many more to become defaulters," Mahbubur Rahman, a former president of the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industries (FBCCI), told Reuters.
STATE INDUSTRIES' LOSSES ROSE
Losses of state-owned industries mounted even though they received more than 20 billion taka in government subsidies in 1995/96 alone.
"There was a little breathing space for local industries to adjust to competition. The tariff wall was lowered drastically without matching reforms in policies and facilities," Rahman said.

"It's now useless to debate on liberalisation after (the creation of) the World Trade Organisation (WTO). We have to integrate with the global economy whether we want it or not. The faster we could move, the better," one exporter said.
One revenue official said local industries still had effective tariff protection of five percent to 15 percent.

"We are constantly keeping duties of raw materials lower than finished products," the official said. "In fact, it's a transition period for Bangladeshi industry. Not everybody is losing. Some sector have come out very strongly."
Sectors including leather, tableware, detergent and aluminium have won out over foreign goods, market sources said.
Meanwhile, the Finance Ministry has not acted on a call by the World Bank, which is guiding Bangladesh's trade reform, to lower the highest customs duty to 30 percent from 45 percent.

"It's unlikely at the moment. We have gone quite fast in recent years. It's not only protection to domestic industries that matters. Dwindling revenue from imports is also a concern," said the revenue official.
